title: Trump: A dozen Trump officials resign following the Capitol attack
description_short: Trump: A dozen Trump officials resign following the Capitol attack
description_medium: In the first day after the January 6 Capitol attack, at least 12 Trump administration officials resigned. Some departures were described as protests over the violence. Education Secretary Betsy DeVos said the president’s rhetoric had contributed to the crisis; her resignation took effect January 8. Transportation Secretary Elaine Chao also announced she was leaving. DeVos’s departure meant she would not have to decide whether to support invoking the Twenty-Fifth Amendment.
description_long:
At least 12 officials left the Trump administration during the first 24 hours after a mob attacked the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021. The departures did not all carry the same stated motive: some officials resigned in protest, while Education Secretary Betsy DeVos also avoided a possible Cabinet vote on invoking the Twenty-Fifth Amendment to remove President Donald Trump from office. DeVos wrote that Trump’s rhetoric had affected the situation and called the violence unconscionable; her resignation became effective January 8. Transportation Secretary Elaine Chao announced her resignation earlier that day.

The timing made the resignations a measure of the pressure inside the administration after the attack and the effort to resume Congress’s work of certifying the election. They were individual exits, not a collective Cabinet decision, and the account does not establish that enough officials supported using the Twenty-Fifth Amendment. The distinction matters: leaving office expressed opposition or avoided a decision, but it did not itself remove the president or settle questions about responsibility for the attack. The episode exposed disagreement within Trump’s own government over his conduct and the response to the violence.

title: Trump: DOJ fights against law that protects children from abuse
description_short: Trump: DOJ fights against law that protects children from abuse
description_medium: The Justice Department moved to intervene in litigation over a Washington state law requiring churches to report child-abuse allegations within 48 hours. State lawmakers passed the reporting requirement in May 2025, and the case sought to amend it as it applied to priests. The filing placed the federal government on the side of a legal challenge to the state’s reporting rule. The supplied account does not specify the DOJ’s legal arguments or the case’s outcome.
description_long:
In June 2025, the U.S. Department of Justice filed a motion to intervene in a Washington case concerning a state law on reporting child abuse. The legislature had passed a measure in May requiring churches to report allegations to authorities within 48 hours. The lawsuit sought to amend the law as it applied to priests, and the DOJ’s motion made the federal department a participant in that dispute. The available account does not describe the department’s precise legal arguments, identify the plaintiffs, or report a ruling, so this filing should not be treated as a final decision about the law.

The dispute concerns how a state’s mandatory-reporting requirement applies within religious institutions and whether the rule should be changed for clergy. A federal motion to intervene can affect how a case is argued and whose position the court hears, but the filing alone does not establish the eventual scope of the reporting duty. The event is notable because the Trump administration’s DOJ entered a case involving protections for children and a state effort to require prompt reporting. The legal consequences remained unresolved in the information supplied for this entry.

title: Trump: FBI subpoenas Trump over deal with John Cody, mob associate
description_short: Trump: FBI subpoenas Trump over deal with John Cody, mob associate

The available account does not say that the subpoena resulted in a charge or establish that Trump committed a crime.
description_long:
The FBI subpoenaed Donald Trump sometime in 1980 while investigating John Cody, a racketeer and New York mob associate who had business ties to Trump and Roy Cohn. Cody was president of Teamsters Local 282, the union supplying concrete for the construction of Trump Tower. That connection brought a labor organization involved in a major building project into the orbit of a federal investigation of alleged organized-crime activity. The account describes a subpoena issued to Trump; it does not say that he was charged, that investigators established he knew of criminal conduct, or that the investigation produced a finding against him.

The episode is relevant to the history of Trump’s business relationships and to the scrutiny surrounding construction contracting in New York, but the supplied material does not provide the subpoena’s contents, Trump’s response, or the investigation’s final result. title: Trump: FBI Director Chris Wray announces leave ahead of Trump inauguration
description_short: Trump: FBI Director Chris Wray announces leave ahead of Trump inauguration
description_medium: FBI Director Christopher Wray announced that he would leave at the end of President Joe Biden’s term, before Donald Trump returned to office. Trump had said he planned to nominate Kash Patel to lead the bureau, and Wray’s departure cleared the way for a successor without Trump first having to remove him. Trump had appointed Wray in 2017 to a 10-year term. The announcement did not itself confirm Patel’s nomination or appointment.
description_long:
FBI Director Christopher Wray announced on December 11, 2024, that he would step down at the end of Joe Biden’s term. Donald Trump had said he planned to nominate Kash Patel to head the bureau. Wray had been appointed by Trump in 2017 to a 10-year term, so his decision to leave early made it easier for the incoming president to install a new director without first removing the incumbent. The announcement was a decision by Wray; it did not itself amount to a formal nomination or Senate confirmation of Patel.

The event drew attention to the transition of leadership at the FBI, an agency whose director’s term is designed to extend beyond a single presidential term. The supplied account links Wray’s departure to Trump’s stated successor plan, but does not establish that political pressure caused Wray to resign. Keeping those points separate matters: the timing changed the practical path for a new administration, while the reasons for Wray’s choice and the subsequent confirmation process are not described here. The immediate consequence was that Trump would face a vacancy rather than the need to displace a sitting director.
notes: Completed from the assigned synopsis and the linked AP report metadata; no claim is made that Patel had already been formally nominated.

title: Trump DOJ launches politicized investigation against Federal Reserve Chair Powell
description_short: Trump DOJ launches politicized investigation against Federal Reserve Chair Powell

The criminal investigation concerned Powell’s June 2025 testimony to the Senate Banking Committee about a Federal Reserve renovation project. President Trump had repeatedly criticized Powell and discussed removing him. The supplied account does not establish that the investigation was improper or report its outcome; the overlap raised questions about political pressure on the central bank.
description_long:
The U.S. attorney’s office in Washington, D.C., served grand jury subpoenas on Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell on January 9, 2026. The investigation concerned Powell’s testimony to the Senate Banking Committee in June 2025 about the Federal Reserve’s renovation project. The subpoenas indicated that prosecutors were seeking information as part of a criminal inquiry; they did not by themselves establish that Powell had committed an offense. The entry places the investigation in the context of President Donald Trump’s repeated public criticism of Powell and his earlier statements entertaining the idea of removing him.

That timing matters because the Federal Reserve’s ability to set monetary policy independently of day-to-day political direction is central to how the institution is understood. An investigation touching its chair can therefore prompt scrutiny of whether law enforcement is being used to influence an agency, especially amid a public dispute between the president and the chair. The supplied information, however, does not establish that Trump directed the investigation, disclose the prosecutors’ evidence, or say what happened after the subpoenas.
